mcqs.question: What is the space complexity of building a frequency table over n items, and why?
options: O(n), because you must store one entry per input item regardless of duplicates
O(1), because hashmaps have constant space by definition
O(k), where k is the number of distinct values — space scales with unique values, not total items
O(log n), because hashmap entries are stored in a balanced tree
mcqs.explanation: A frequency table has one entry per distinct value, not per input element, so repeated values cost nothing extra in space — only the count they update. Hashmaps have no inherent O(1) space guarantee and aren't tree-based by default.

mcqs.question: In an anagram check that increments counts on string s and decrements on string t, why return False the moment a count goes negative, instead of comparing full tables at the end?
options: A negative count means t has already used more of that character than s has, so a match is impossible regardless of what's still unscanned
Negative counts are a signal that the table needs to be resized
It's required to keep the algorithm at O(1) additional space
It only works correctly when the two strings contain no repeated characters
mcqs.explanation: Once t has consumed more of a character than s ever contributed, no later characters can undo that deficit, so returning early is a correctness shortcut, not a space or resizing concern.

mcqs.question: Why does Boyer-Moore voting correctly find the majority element using only O(1) extra space?
options: It sorts the array first so the majority element ends up in the middle
It relies on a guaranteed true majority — appearing more than n/2 times — surviving repeated cancellation against every other value combined
It builds a full frequency table but discards all counts except the highest
It only works correctly when there are exactly two distinct values in the array
mcqs.explanation: Because a true majority element outnumbers everything else combined, it can never be fully cancelled out by the counter dropping to zero, which is what lets a single candidate-and-counter pair track it without a table. No sorting or frequency table is involved, and it works for any number of distinct values as long as a true majority exists.

mcqs.question: Why does bucket-sort-by-frequency solve Top-K Frequent Elements in O(n), where sorting values by count costs O(k log k)?
options: It skips building a frequency table entirely
It only produces correct results when k equals 1
Frequency can never exceed n, so an array of n+1 buckets can hold every distinct value at its exact count, avoiding any sorting comparison
It relies on the input already being sorted by frequency
mcqs.explanation: Bounding frequency by n means bucket indices are bounded too, so placing values into buckets and scanning from the top is linear — no comparisons needed the way a sort requires. It still builds a frequency table first; that step just isn't the bottleneck.

mcqs.question: Why would you choose a min-heap of size k over bucket-sort-by-frequency for a Top-K Frequent Elements variant where data arrives as an unbounded stream?
options: A min-heap is always asymptotically faster than bucket sort in every case
Bucket sort needs n known upfront to size its bucket array, while a heap of fixed size k naturally caps memory as unbounded data streams in
A min-heap eliminates the need to build a frequency table at all
Bucket sort cannot represent ties in frequency correctly
mcqs.explanation: A bucket array is sized by the maximum possible frequency, which needs a known n; a size-k heap instead just evicts the smallest count whenever it grows past k, which fits a stream of unknown length. Bucket sort is actually the asymptotically faster option on a fixed array, and both approaches still need a frequency table underneath.

mcqs.question: Why does First Unique Character need a second pass over the string in original order, instead of answering directly from the frequency table?
options: Because the frequency table doesn't store characters in their original sorted order
Because a hashmap can't store counts larger than 1 for any key
Because the frequency table tells you which characters are unique but not which one appears first — that requires scanning in original order
Because building a frequency table only works for lowercase letters
mcqs.explanation: A hashmap has no concept of the input's original position, so finding which unique character comes first needs a second, position-aware pass — the table alone can answer "is this unique," not "where is it."
